author: CATIE HARPER Daily News-Record
title: Five turnovers doom JMU football in second consecutive overtime loss | James Madison University | dnronline.com
text:
James Madison was staring down a fourth-and-1 in its second overtime period in as many weeks.
With a decision to make, head coach Billy Napier kept his offense on the field.
It’s what the analytics said to do, and in theory, it was a situation the Dukes have handled well this season.
But with it all on the line, running back Seth Cromwell came up short of the first-down marker.
A change of possession and several plays later, Troy kicker Hayden Wolfe took the field.
A 27-yard boot through the uprights and the game was over.
The Trojans stormed the field. The Dukes were left silent on the sidelines.
For the second consecutive week, JMU lost in overtime — this time falling 24-21 to one of its two Sun Belt West opponents.
“We felt like we could get a yard,” Napier said. “I do think, you know, that we had conviction about that, and we went for it. … It's fourth-and-1, and analytically speaking, it's the right decision, and I think based off how the game was going, it was the right decision.”
JMU’s overtime loss once again came after the Dukes built a multi-score lead to open the game.
As the JMU faithful have seen throughout the season, the Dukes have the opening possessions down.
The ones that come after?
Well, those have been questionable at best.
In their return to Bridgeforth Stadium after suffering their first loss of the season, the Dukes ended their first possession in a familiar area — the end zone.
It was a similar story for two other first-half possessions, but as the game progressed, JMU’s offensive drives got shorter and shorter.
Passes were intercepted.
Footballs ended up on the ground after long receptions, with the visiting Trojans falling on them.
The miscues piled up, and the Dukes were left to watch their 21-7 halftime lead quickly slip away.
“Consistency, turnovers, fumbles, all that,” Cromwell said. “Penalties … A lot of self-violence. Like, when we — we lost the game, really, that was it. And then, you know, five turnovers, just terrible.”
For the majority of Thursday night’s clash, JMU’s defense did what it was supposed to do.
The Dukes held the Trojans’ offense to just one touchdown in the first half, and even Troy's 1-yard score from running back Gavin Griffin came with some help from JMU.
The Dukes committed three penalties on Troy’s first scoring drive, including pass interference and roughing the passer calls that helped extend the possession.
“We have a handful of penalties in key moments,” Napier said. “It's just not good enough to win.”
Following the Trojans’ first touchdown, they failed to score again until the third quarter.
And when Troy finally found its way back to the end zone, it wasn't the fault of JMU’s defense.
Quarterback JC Evans, who was splitting reps with Camden Coleman, put a pass in the hands of Troy safety Justin Powe.
The fifth-year defender found his way to the sideline, tiptoed along the boundary and reached the end zone to cut JMU’s lead to 21-14.
“We turned the ball over,” Napier said. “One of those is a pick-6. You know, our defense played well enough to win. Cumulative effect wore down a little bit in the second half, but you're not going to win games when you turn the ball over five times.”
Powe’s touchdown silenced an already dwindling home crowd, and JMU’s offense did little to bring it back during its ensuing possessions.
The Dukes’ struggles on offense gave Troy just what it needed — time.
JMU’s defense was forced to spend extended periods on the field, and it finally showed a crack as the third quarter progressed.
Much to the Dukes’ dismay, the Trojans’ third touchdown came after another turnover.
Evans hit receiver Jeremiah Harrison for a 14-yard completion, but the second-year player couldn’t keep the ball in his hands. Harrison’s fumble was recovered by Troy’s Miquon Merriweather at JMU’s 42-yard line.
It was one of five JMU turnovers in the game. The Dukes threw three interceptions and lost two fumbles.
Troy capitalized on Harrison’s mistake, piecing together a three-play scoring drive. The Trojans capped it with a 28-yard touchdown run from Jaheim Merriweather to tie the game at 21.
“Tonight was turnovers,” Napier said. “I mean, I think we moved the ball up and down the field and shot ourselves in the foot and turned the ball over.”
Troy’s second-half surge quickly negated the lead the Dukes built during the first half.
JMU opened Thursday with another quick score, something it has done in all but two games this season.
After Troy turned the ball over on downs, Coleman quickly led the offense down the field for a first-possession touchdown.
Cromwell, who got the start for an injured George Pettaway, had four carries for 31 yards on the drive. Coleman punched in the touchdown on fourth-and-2 to give the Dukes a 7-0 lead.
The fourth-year quarterback helped the Dukes double their advantage before the Trojans found their first points of the evening.
Coleman connected with receiver Braeden Wisloski for a 31-yard touchdown that gave JMU a 14-0 edge.
The score was Wisloski’s second of the season.
After Troy cut JMU’s lead to 14-7 with Griffin’s 1-yard score, the Dukes didn’t miss a beat.
Evans took over at quarterback and crafted a 12-play, 75-yard scoring drive.
JMU’s longest play on the possession was a 19-yard completion to receiver Noah Grevious on third-and-14, but it was Cromwell who finished it on the ground. The running back broke free for a 14-yard touchdown run to reestablish JMU’s 14-point lead.
Cromwell’s rushing score quickly took a backseat to what the offense failed to do afterward.
JMU scored on its first three possessions of the game, but from there, 13 consecutive drives ended with either a punt or turnover.
Both JMU quarterbacks threw at least one interception, with Coleman throwing two. Harrison and receiver Michael Scott each lost a fumble after a first-down reception.
Troy had its own turnover during JMU’s run of poor offensive possessions, but the Dukes failed to capitalize after defensive lineman Kells Bush forced a fumble that was recovered by edge Turner Schmidt.
JMU's offense ran just five plays before being forced to punt following the takeaway.
“It's really hard to put into words,” Cromwell said. “You work through practice, you don't see it all week at practice, and then it gets to the game and then everything goes out the window.”
JMU was driving as the game neared its end, crossing into Troy territory with time still left on the clock.
Regulation ended on a failed Hail Mary attempt to tight end Cole Keller, who got his hands on the ball but couldn’t control it to the ground.
Napier said postgame that JMU was trying to position itself for a field goal, but the Dukes' run plays failed to gain the yardage they needed.
“We were working on first, second and third down to try to see if we could position for a field goal,” Napier said. “The kick line was the 33. We were on the 37, and the two runs on first and second down weren't efficient.”
Coleman finished 14 of 25 for 147 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions. Evans was 8 of 10 for 72 yards and an interception.
Cromwell led JMU on the ground with 23 carries for 135 yards and a touchdown.
Defensively, JMU safety TJ McGill, linebacker Nakian Jackson and defensive lineman Rasheed Lovelace each finished with seven tackles.
The Dukes will now hit the road for one final Thursday night game, traveling to Southern Mississippi in hopes of snapping their two-game skid.
For McGill, the answer to consecutive overtime losses starts with making sure the Dukes don't allow them to pull the team apart.
“Stick together as a team,” McGill said. “The relationships that we built since the spring, we just got to just hold on to that and just go back to the drawing board and figure out what we got to do to get better and focus on the next opponent.”

The Dukes committed three penalties on Troy’s first scoring drive, including pass interference and roughing the passer calls that helped extend the possession. Quarterback JC Evans, who was splitting reps with Camden Coleman, put a pass in the hands of Troy safety Justin Powe.
